# Sound as Text

## In this particular phrase, that is indeed the case. However, my definition is more low-level, since it includes elements of the non-linguistic, specifically the sonic — let's call it phonetic — part. Although, in truth, phonetics does not consider the entire aspect of sound as a level of pre-language, which is likewise an information-rich object.

## Since human sound arises not only from the work of the mouth but also, for example, from the movement of the tongue, virtually any part of the body can be its source. A person can make sounds by blinking frequently and flapping their eyes, or, for example, through the action of the stomach sphincter. That is why the study of sound — and, accordingly, of music — involves a decidedly non-trivial level of complexity.

## Anything can produce sounds, but interpreting them is quite another matter. The study of sound goes beyond any structure of linguistics, since studying language as a limited form restricts the possibility of knowing the whole spectrum of ways to convey one's own reaction.

## That is why musical notation exists. But there is still no sound aggregation, owing to the extreme complexity of analyzing noise.

## But why write sound down as text at all? Sound is sound: it should be heard, not read. Now imagine that, thanks to such notation, a person who hears nothing could understand what sound is in front of them. Or, for example, someone who cannot interpret a sound because they lack the relevant knowledge would get the chance to understand it.
